name: Full stack developer core vocabulary
description: The 100 terms a full stack developer needs to know, from the web basics to architecture and reliability.

cards.subject: HTTP
says: is the request and response protocol that browsers and servers use to exchange web content
is stateless, so each request stands alone
cards.use: need to explain how a browser asks a server for a page
not: encrypts every request by default

cards.subject: status code
says: is a three-digit number in a response that tells the client how the request went
groups results by first digit, such as 2xx for success and 4xx for client errors
cards.use: see 404 or 500 returned by a server
not: is chosen by the browser rather than the server

cards.subject: HTTP method
says: tells the server what action is wanted on a resource
includes GET to read, POST to create and DELETE to remove
cards.use: need to say whether a request reads or changes data
not: is a number that shows whether a request succeeded

cards.subject: header
says: carries extra information about a request or response as name and value pairs
can tell the server the content type or carry an authorisation token
cards.use: need to send metadata such as the content type with a request
not: holds the main body of the page

cards.subject: cookie
says: is a small piece of data that a server asks the browser to store and send back
is often used to keep a user logged in
cards.use: need the browser to remember who the user is across requests
not: is always deleted as soon as the tab is closed

cards.subject: DNS
says: translates a domain name into an IP address
is consulted before a browser can contact a server by name
cards.use: need to point a domain name at a server
not: encrypts traffic between the browser and the server

cards.subject: TLS
says: encrypts traffic between a client and a server
is what turns HTTP into HTTPS
cards.use: need to stop others reading traffic while it is in transit
not: converts a domain name into an IP address

cards.subject: CDN
says: serves copies of content from servers close to the user
reduces load on the origin server and speeds up delivery of static files
cards.use: want images and scripts delivered quickly to users around the world
not: stores the main database for the site

cards.subject: CORS
says: is a browser mechanism that lets a server say which other origins may read its responses
blocks a page from reading a response from another origin unless the server allows it
cards.use: see a browser block a request from your front end to a different domain
not: is a server-side firewall that blocks all traffic from other countries

cards.subject: WebSocket
says: keeps a two-way connection open between a browser and a server
lets the server push messages without waiting for a request
cards.use: need live updates such as a chat or a price feed
not: sends a new request each time the data is wanted

cards.subject: DOM
says: is the browser's tree-shaped model of a page that scripts can read and change
represents each element of the HTML as a node
cards.use: need to change what is on the page from JavaScript
not: is a language for describing how a page looks

cards.subject: semantic HTML
says: uses elements that describe the meaning of content, such as nav and article
helps screen readers and search engines understand a page
cards.use: want a page that assistive technology can navigate
not: uses only div elements for every part of the layout

cards.subject: responsive design
says: adapts a layout to different screen sizes
often uses flexible grids and media queries
cards.use: need one site to work on phones and on desktops
not: builds a separate site for each device

cards.subject: accessibility
says: makes a site usable by people with disabilities
covers keyboard use, screen readers, colour contrast and alternative text
cards.use: need people who use only a keyboard or a screen reader to use the site
not: only matters for visitors who use mobile phones

cards.subject: component
says: is a reusable piece of interface with its own markup, logic and style
can be combined with others to build a page
cards.use: need to reuse the same button or card in many places
not: is a database table that stores page content

cards.subject: state
says: is the data in an interface that can change over time
triggers an update to the interface when it changes
cards.use: need an interface to update when a user toggles something
not: is the fixed markup that never changes

cards.subject: server-side rendering
says: builds the HTML for a page on the server before sending it
gives the browser content to show before the JavaScript has loaded
cards.use: want search engines and users to receive full content on the first load
not: builds the whole page in the browser from an empty HTML shell

cards.subject: client-side rendering
says: builds the page in the browser using JavaScript
often starts from an almost empty HTML shell
cards.use: need a highly interactive app that runs mainly in the browser
not: sends fully built HTML from the server for each page

cards.subject: hydration
says: attaches JavaScript behaviour to HTML that was already rendered on the server
makes server-rendered markup interactive
cards.use: have server-rendered HTML that now needs click handlers
not: removes JavaScript from a page to make it faster

cards.subject: bundler
says: combines and optimises source files into fewer files for the browser
can split code so users load only what they need
cards.use: need to ship many modules as optimised files
not: runs the database migrations

cards.subject: API
says: is a defined way for one piece of software to ask another for data or actions
hides how the other system works internally
cards.use: need your front end to get data from the server
not: is a type of database

cards.subject: REST
says: is a style of API built around resources and standard HTTP methods
treats each URL as a resource that clients read or change
cards.use: need to design an API around resources such as users and orders
not: requires clients to write a query that picks the exact fields they want

cards.subject: GraphQL
says: lets a client ask for exactly the fields it needs in one query
exposes a typed schema that describes what can be queried
cards.use: need clients to choose which fields come back and avoid several round trips
not: gives every resource its own fixed URL as its main design idea

cards.subject: endpoint
says: is a specific URL where an API receives requests
combines with an HTTP method to define one operation
cards.use: need to name the exact address that a client calls
not: is the final step of a deployment

cards.subject: middleware
says: runs between the incoming request and the final handler
is used for things like logging, authentication and parsing
cards.use: need to run the same check on every request
not: stores data between server restarts

cards.subject: webhook
says: is a call that one system makes to a URL of yours when an event happens
pushes events to you instead of making you poll for them
cards.use: need to be told when a payment succeeds without checking repeatedly
not: is a request that your code makes on a schedule to check for changes

cards.subject: rate limiting
says: caps how many requests a client may make in a period
protects a service from overload and abuse
cards.use: need to stop one client flooding the API
not: sorts requests into the order they arrived

cards.subject: idempotency
says: means repeating the same request has the same effect as making it once
makes it safe to retry after a timeout
cards.use: need a payment request to be safe to retry
not: means a request can never be sent twice

cards.subject: pagination
says: splits a large result into pages that a client requests one at a time
keeps responses small and fast
cards.use: need an endpoint to return thousands of records without sending them all at once
not: encrypts the results of a query

cards.subject: background job
says: runs work outside the request that triggered it
is often placed on a queue and processed by a worker
cards.use: need to send emails without making the user wait
not: blocks the response until all of the work is finished

cards.subject: schema
says: describes the structure of a database, including tables, columns and types
defines what shape the stored data must have
cards.use: need to define the tables and columns for an application
not: is a copy of the data kept in case of loss

cards.subject: primary key
says: uniquely identifies each row in a table
cannot be empty or duplicated
cards.use: need a way to identify each record exactly
not: points at a row in another table

cards.subject: foreign key
says: is a column that refers to the primary key of another table
keeps the link between related records consistent
cards.use: need an order row to point at the customer who placed it
not: uniquely identifies each row in its own table

cards.subject: index
says: speeds up lookups on a column by keeping a sorted structure
makes writes slightly slower
cards.use: see a slow query that filters on one column
not: is a column that must hold a unique value

cards.subject: join
says: combines rows from two tables based on a related column
returns data that is stored in separate tables
cards.use: need customer names alongside their orders
not: adds a new column to a table

cards.subject: migration
says: is a versioned change to the database schema
can be applied in order and tracked in source control
cards.use: need to add a column to the production database safely
not: is a one-off copy of production data to a laptop

cards.subject: transaction
says: groups several database operations so that they all succeed or all fail
protects data from being left half-updated
cards.use: need to move money between two accounts without losing either side
not: speeds up a query by sorting the data

cards.subject: ORM
says: maps database tables to objects in code
lets developers query with code instead of hand-written SQL
cards.use: want to work with database rows as objects
not: encrypts the values stored in columns

cards.subject: NoSQL
says: describes databases that do not use fixed tables and relational joins by default
includes document, key-value and graph stores
cards.use: need flexible documents rather than fixed tables
not: is a newer version of the SQL language

cards.subject: cache
says: keeps a copy of costly-to-get data in fast storage
speeds up repeated reads but can serve stale data
cards.use: see the same expensive query run again and again
not: is the permanent copy of record for the data

cards.subject: authentication
says: proves who a user is
is usually done with a password, a token or another factor
cards.use: need to check that the person logging in is who they claim to be
not: decides what a user is allowed to do

cards.subject: authorisation
says: decides what an authenticated user is allowed to do
controls access to resources and actions
cards.use: need to stop ordinary users opening admin pages
not: proves who a user is

cards.subject: hashing
says: turns data into a fixed-size value that cannot practically be reversed
is the right way to store passwords, together with a salt
cards.use: need to store passwords safely
not: scrambles data so that it can be decrypted later with a key

cards.subject: encryption
says: scrambles data so that only someone with the key can read it
can be reversed with the right key
cards.use: need to protect data so that the right people can read it later
not: produces a value that cannot practically be reversed

cards.subject: cross-site scripting
says: lets an attacker run their script in another user's browser through your page
is prevented by escaping or sanitising output
cards.use: find that user comments are inserted into a page without being escaped
not: tricks a logged-in user's browser into sending an unwanted request

cards.subject: CSRF
says: tricks a logged-in user's browser into making an unwanted request
is reduced with anti-forgery tokens and same-site cookies
cards.use: worry that a malicious site could make a user's browser submit a form to your site
not: injects attacker script into your own page

cards.subject: SQL injection
says: lets an attacker change a database query through unsafe input
is prevented by parameterised queries
cards.use: see user input joined straight into a query string
not: steals a session cookie through a script in the page

cards.subject: OAuth
says: lets a user give an app limited access to their account without sharing the password
issues access tokens with a set scope
cards.use: need a user to let your app read their calendar without giving you their password
not: is a method of hashing passwords

cards.subject: least privilege
says: gives each user or service only the access it needs
limits the damage when an account is compromised
cards.use: need to decide how much access a service account should have
not: gives every developer full admin access for speed

cards.subject: secrets management
says: keeps passwords, keys and tokens out of source code
stores them in a controlled place and rotates them
cards.use: find an API key committed to a repository
not: puts every key in the code so that nothing is lost

cards.subject: repository
says: stores a project's files and their full history
can be local or hosted on a service
cards.use: need a place that keeps a project's code and its history
not: is a single saved change

cards.subject: commit
says: records a snapshot of changes with a message
forms a point in history that can be returned to
cards.use: need to save a set of changes with a description
not: is a separate line of development

cards.subject: branch
says: is a separate line of development
lets work happen without affecting the main code
cards.use: need to work on a feature without disturbing the main code
not: is a permanent label on one release

cards.subject: pull request
says: proposes merging one branch into another
is where teammates review and discuss changes
cards.use: need others to review your work before it is merged
not: downloads the latest changes from the remote repository

cards.subject: code review
says: is when teammates examine changes before they are merged
catches bugs and shares knowledge
cards.use: want a second pair of eyes on your change
not: is an automated tool that formats code

cards.subject: merge conflict
says: happens when two changes touch the same lines and git cannot combine them
needs a person to choose the correct result
cards.use: see git refuse to combine two branches that edit the same lines
not: happens when a repository is deleted

cards.subject: rebase
says: replays a branch's commits on top of another base
gives a cleaner linear history but rewrites commits
cards.use: want your feature branch to sit on top of the latest main
not: joins two histories with a new merge commit

cards.subject: tag
says: marks a specific commit, often a release
does not move as new commits are added
cards.use: need to mark exactly what shipped as version 2.0
not: is a branch that moves with each new commit

cards.subject: fork
says: is a personal copy of someone else's repository
lets you propose changes without write access to the original
cards.use: want to contribute to a project that you cannot write to
not: is a branch inside the same repository

cards.subject: monorepo
says: keeps the code for many projects in one repository
makes sharing code and changing several projects at once easier
cards.use: need to change a shared library and all of its users in one commit
not: gives every service its own repository

cards.subject: unit test
says: checks one small piece of code in isolation
runs fast and pinpoints where a failure is
cards.use: want to check one function quickly
not: tests the whole system through the browser

cards.subject: integration test
says: checks that several parts work together
may use a real database or service
cards.use: need to confirm that the API and the database work together
not: checks a single function with all of its dependencies replaced

cards.subject: end-to-end test
says: drives the whole application as a user would
covers the full path from the interface to the data
cards.use: need to check that login, checkout and email all work together
not: checks one function in isolation

cards.subject: test coverage
says: measures how much of the code is run by the tests
does not prove that the tests check the right things
cards.use: want to know which code no test touches
not: measures how fast the tests run

cards.subject: regression
says: is a bug where something that used to work stops working
is guarded against by automated tests
cards.use: find that an old feature broke after a new change
not: is a new feature added to a product

cards.subject: mock
says: replaces a real dependency with a controlled fake in a test
lets a test run without calling a real service
cards.use: need to test code that calls a payment service without really charging anyone
not: is a test that runs against production data

cards.subject: linting
says: analyses code for likely errors and style problems without running it
catches issues before review
cards.use: want unused variables and style slips caught automatically
not: runs the application and clicks through it

cards.subject: type checking
says: checks that values are used in ways their types allow
catches mismatches before the code runs
cards.use: want mistakes such as passing a string where a number is needed caught early
not: measures how many lines are covered by tests

cards.subject: refactoring
says: restructures code without changing what it does
makes code easier to understand and change
cards.use: need to tidy code without changing its behaviour
not: adds new features while the code is being rewritten

cards.subject: technical debt
says: is the future cost of shortcuts taken in design or code
builds up when quick fixes are never revisited
cards.use: see old shortcuts slowing down every change
not: is money owed to a software supplier

cards.subject: continuous integration
says: merges and tests code changes automatically and often
catches broken builds soon after a change
cards.use: want every push to be built and tested automatically
not: releases every change to users automatically

cards.subject: continuous delivery
says: keeps software always in a state that can be released
automates the steps up to the release
cards.use: want any good build to be ready to release at the push of a button
not: runs tests only on one developer's machine

cards.subject: staging environment
says: is a copy of production used to test changes before release
should be as like production as possible
cards.use: need to try a release before real users see it
not: is the live environment that customers use

cards.subject: container
says: packages an application with what it needs to run
runs the same way on different machines
cards.use: need an app to run identically on a laptop and a server
not: is a full virtual computer with its own operating system kernel

cards.subject: rollback
says: returns a system to a previous working version
is the first thing to consider when a release breaks production
cards.use: see a new release break production
not: adds new features to a release that is already live

cards.subject: feature flag
says: switches a feature on or off without a new deployment
lets code be released but kept hidden
cards.use: want to release code but show it to only some users
not: marks a bug as fixed in the tracker

cards.subject: infrastructure as code
says: describes servers and networks in files kept in version control
makes environments repeatable
cards.use: need to recreate the same environment reliably
not: means setting servers up by hand using a console

cards.subject: serverless
says: runs code on a platform that manages the servers
scales with demand and is billed by use
cards.use: want to run small functions without managing servers
not: means the code runs with no computer involved

cards.subject: load balancer
says: spreads incoming requests across several servers
can stop sending traffic to a server that has failed
cards.use: need to share traffic between several servers
not: translates domain names into IP addresses

cards.subject: blue-green deployment
says: keeps two identical environments and switches traffic from one to the other
allows an instant switch back if the new version fails
cards.use: want a release with almost no downtime and an instant fallback
not: updates servers one at a time in place with no spare environment

cards.subject: latency
says: is the time a request takes to get a response
is affected by distance, the work done and waiting
cards.use: hear users say that pages feel slow
not: is the number of requests handled per second

cards.subject: throughput
says: is how much work a system handles in a given time
is often measured in requests per second
cards.use: need to know how many requests a service can handle each second
not: is the time that one request takes

cards.subject: horizontal scaling
says: adds more machines to share the load
needs the application not to depend on one machine's memory
cards.use: need to handle more traffic by adding servers
not: adds more CPU and memory to a single machine

cards.subject: logging
says: records events as an application runs
helps explain what happened after a failure
cards.use: need a record of what the application did before it failed
not: checks values against the types they should have

cards.subject: monitoring
says: watches the health of a system through metrics and alerts
tells a team when something is wrong
cards.use: need to know when the error rate rises
not: stores every message the application writes

cards.subject: observability
says: lets a team understand a system's internal state from its outputs
combines logs, metrics and traces
cards.use: need to find why a request was slow across several services
not: is a list of scheduled releases

cards.subject: service level objective
says: is a target for how reliable a service should be
is measured against an indicator such as availability
cards.use: need to say how reliable a service should be
not: is a legal contract that carries penalties

cards.subject: post-incident review
says: looks at what happened after an outage and why
aims to learn without blaming individuals
cards.use: have just fixed an outage and want to stop it happening again
not: decides which engineer should be disciplined

cards.subject: race condition
says: is a bug where the result depends on the unpredictable timing of events
can appear only occasionally
cards.use: see a bug that appears only when two requests arrive at nearly the same moment
not: is a bug that always occurs on the first request

cards.subject: memory leak
says: is memory that is never released so that usage grows over time
can make a long-running service slow or crash
cards.use: see a server's memory use rise until it falls over
not: is a bug that depends on the timing of two requests

cards.subject: user story
says: describes a feature from the user's point of view
is often written as 'as a user, I want ..., so that ...'
cards.use: need to describe a feature in terms of what a user wants
not: is a technical design for the database

cards.subject: sprint
says: is a fixed short period in which a team works on agreed items
ends with a review and a retrospective
cards.use: need to plan two weeks of work
not: is a list of everything that might be built

cards.subject: backlog
says: is the ordered list of work a team might do
is re-ordered as priorities change
cards.use: need a list of everything still to build, in priority order
not: is the fixed set of work agreed for one sprint

cards.subject: definition of done
says: is the shared checklist that work must meet to count as finished
covers things like tests, review and documentation
cards.use: need agreement on what finished means
not: is the date on which a project must end

cards.subject: MVP
says: is the smallest version of a product that delivers value and teaches the team something
is used to test an idea before building more
cards.use: want to test an idea with real users before building everything
not: is the final polished version with every planned feature

cards.subject: monolith
says: is an application built and deployed as one unit
keeps all of its code in one codebase and process
cards.use: have one application that is deployed as a single piece
not: splits an application into many independently deployed services

cards.subject: microservice architecture
says: splits an application into many small, independently deployed services
lets teams release parts of the system separately
cards.use: need teams to deploy parts of a system on their own schedules
not: deploys the whole application as one unit

cards.subject: architecture decision record
says: is a short document capturing an important design decision and why it was made
lets later developers see the reasoning
cards.use: need to record why the team chose one design over another
not: is a diagram of the servers

cards.subject: breaking change
says: is a change that makes existing users of an API or library stop working
calls for a new version or a migration path
cards.use: need to rename a field that other clients rely on
not: is a fix that makes no difference to anyone

cards.subject: event-driven architecture
says: has parts of a system react to events rather than call each other directly
lets producers and consumers work independently
cards.use: need services to react to things that happen, such as an order being placed
not: has every service call the others and wait for an answer

qa.q: What does the status code 404 mean?
qa.right: The requested resource was not found
wrong: The user is not logged in
qa.why: 404 means the server could not find what was asked for.

qa.q: Which HTTP method is normally used to read data?
qa.why: GET reads; the others create, change or remove.

qa.q: What does DNS do?
qa.right: Translates a domain name into an IP address
wrong: Encrypts traffic between browser and server
qa.why: DNS turns names into addresses.

qa.q: Which of these is a primary key?
qa.right: A column that uniquely identifies each row
wrong: A column that links to another table
A sorted structure that speeds up lookups
A copy of the whole table
qa.why: A primary key identifies each row uniquely.

qa.q: What is a commit?
qa.right: A snapshot of changes saved with a message
wrong: A review of someone else's work
A copy of someone else's repository
qa.why: A commit records a point in history.

qa.q: What does a unit test check?
qa.right: One small piece of code in isolation
wrong: The whole system through the browser
The load on the production servers
How the page looks on a phone
qa.why: Unit tests check one small piece quickly.

qa.q: Why do developers use a branch?
qa.right: To work on a change without disturbing the main code
qa.why: Branches isolate work in progress.

qa.q: A page you changed no longer fits properly on a phone. Which concept is affected?
qa.why: Responsive design adapts layout to screen sizes.

qa.q: Which is the safest way for a database to store a user's password?
qa.right: A salted hash of the password
wrong: The password encrypted with a key kept in the same database
qa.why: Hashing with a salt cannot practically be reversed.

qa.q: A logged-in user who is not an admin opens the admin page and is refused. What decided that?
qa.why: Authorisation decides what an authenticated user may do.

qa.q: Which URL and method most closely follows REST for fetching user 42?
qa.why: REST uses resource URLs and standard methods.

qa.q: Why do teams use pull requests?
qa.right: So that others can review changes before they are merged
wrong: To copy a repository to a new place
qa.why: Pull requests are the place for review and discussion.

qa.q: Where should you try a release before real users see it?
qa.why: Staging mirrors production so releases can be tested safely.

qa.q: Users say a page takes six seconds to respond. Which measure is this?
qa.why: Latency is the time one request takes.

qa.q: A keyboard-only user cannot reach your menu. Which concern is this?
qa.why: Accessibility covers keyboard use and assistive technology.

qa.q: An old feature breaks after a new change. What is this called?
qa.why: A regression is something that used to work and stops.

qa.q: A query that filters on email is slow on a table of millions of rows. What should you consider first?
qa.right: Adding an index on the email column
wrong: Adding more columns to the table
Moving the table into the browser
qa.why: An index speeds up lookups on a column.

qa.q: A marketing page must show full content to search engines on first load. Which rendering suits it?
wrong: Client-side rendering from an empty shell
qa.why: Server-side rendering sends complete HTML.

qa.q: A payment provider tells your server when a payment succeeds. What is the mechanism?
qa.why: A webhook is a call to your URL when an event happens.

qa.q: Git says both branches changed the same lines. What do you do?
qa.right: Open the file, choose or combine the correct lines and commit the resolution
qa.why: A merge conflict needs a person to decide.

qa.q: A release breaks checkout in production. What is the first priority?
qa.right: Restore service, for example by rolling back
wrong: Wait to see if it fixes itself
qa.why: Restoring service comes first.

qa.q: Which practice builds and tests every push automatically?
qa.why: Continuous integration merges and tests often.

qa.q: Product prices change but the page still shows the old ones. What is the likely trade-off?
qa.right: The cache can serve stale data until it is refreshed or invalidated
wrong: The index has become too large
The schema has been migrated twice
The unit tests are not run
qa.why: Caches trade freshness for speed.

qa.q: You need to test code that calls a payment service without really charging anyone. What do you use?
qa.right: A mock of the payment service
qa.why: A mock replaces a real dependency in tests.

qa.q: Clients need to choose exactly which fields come back and avoid several round trips. Which API style helps?
wrong: A fixed set of REST URLs only
qa.why: GraphQL lets the client pick fields in one query.

qa.q: A search endpoint builds its SQL by joining in user text. What is the fix?
qa.why: Parameterised queries prevent SQL injection.

qa.q: A comment containing a script tag runs for other visitors. What is the flaw and the fix?
qa.right: Cross-site scripting; escape or sanitise output
wrong: SQL injection; add a rate limit
qa.why: Unescaped output lets attacker scripts run.

qa.q: A user logged into your site visits a malicious page that submits a transfer. What defends against this?
qa.why: These defend against CSRF.

qa.q: A browser blocks your front end at app.example.com from calling api.example.com. Where is it fixed?
qa.right: The API sends CORS headers that allow the front end's origin
wrong: The browser's JavaScript is switched off
The request is changed to POST
An index is added to the table
qa.why: CORS is configured by the server being called.

qa.q: One client's script sends thousands of requests a minute and slows everyone down. What do you add?
qa.why: Rate limiting caps requests per client.

qa.q: You want to ship code to production but show it only to staff. What do you use?
qa.why: A feature flag switches a feature on or off without a deployment.

qa.q: A transfer debits one account and the server crashes before the credit. Which database feature prevents money disappearing?
qa.why: A transaction makes the group of operations all succeed or all fail.

qa.q: Why should you avoid rebasing a branch others already use?
qa.right: It rewrites commits that other people have built on
wrong: It merges the branch into main
qa.why: Rebasing changes history that others depend on.

qa.q: After adding a second server, users are logged out at random. Sessions were held in the first server's memory. What is the issue?
qa.right: The application depends on one machine's memory, so sessions must move to shared storage
wrong: The CDN is out of date
The database needs a new index
qa.why: Horizontal scaling needs shared state.

qa.q: A request is slow, and it passes through five services. What helps you find which one?
qa.why: Traces show where time is spent across services.

qa.q: You need to rename a response field that mobile apps use. What should you do?
qa.right: Treat it as a breaking change and version the API or keep the old field during a migration
wrong: Rename it and delete the old tests
qa.why: Breaking changes need a migration path.

qa.q: A user lets your app read their calendar without giving you their password. What lets that happen?
qa.why: OAuth grants limited access with tokens.

qa.q: A network times out on a payment request; the client retries and the customer is charged twice. What was missing?
qa.why: Idempotent requests are safe to retry.

qa.q: A reporting service connects with the database admin account. Which principle is broken?
qa.why: Services should have only the access they need.

qa.q: An API key is found in git history. What do you do?
qa.right: Revoke and rotate the key, then remove it from the code
wrong: Delete the file and keep the same key
qa.why: Removing the file does not remove the key from history, so it must be revoked.

qa.q: Two requests both read a stock level of 1 and both sell the last item. What kind of bug is this?
qa.why: The outcome depends on the timing of the requests.

qa.q: A release needs almost no downtime and an instant way back. Which approach fits?
wrong: Editing files directly on the live server
qa.why: Blue-green keeps two environments and switches traffic.

qa.q: Six months later nobody knows why the team chose a queue over direct calls. What would have helped?
qa.why: An ADR captures the reasoning behind a decision.

qa.q: After an outage a manager wants to name who is to blame. What is the better approach?
qa.right: A blameless review that looks at causes and fixes
wrong: Skip the review to save time
qa.why: Blameless reviews help teams learn.

qa.q: A five-person start-up with one product wants twenty microservices. What is a sensible concern?
qa.right: The operational complexity may outweigh the benefits; a monolith may be enough
wrong: Containers cannot run more than one service
qa.why: Microservices add operational cost.

qa.q: A team has skipped tests for months to hit deadlines, and every change is now slower. What is this?
qa.why: Shortcuts build up a future cost.

qa.q: A server's memory use climbs until it crashes, then restarts and does it again. What is the likely problem?
qa.why: Memory that is never released grows over time.

qa.q: Services must react when an order is placed without calling each other directly. Which architecture fits?
qa.why: Services react to events instead of direct calls.

qa.q: Which describes a feature from the user's point of view, such as 'as a user, I want to reset my password'?
qa.why: A user story states what a user wants.
